subject: Biology
title: Cell: The Unit of Life
summary: The cell is the structural and functional unit of every living organism. This chapter builds from the discovery of the cell and the cell theory to the detailed ultrastructure of prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells: the cell envelope, plasma membrane and cell wall, the endomembrane system, mitochondria, plastids, ribosomes, cytoskeleton, cilia and flagella, centrosome, nucleus and chromosomes. It is the base for cell cycle, biomolecules, photosynthesis and respiration in Class 11 and for the whole of molecular biology in Class 12 and NEET, and it is examined almost entirely through labelled diagrams, precise NCERT definitions and comparisons.

exam_profile.weightage: Class 11 Biology is a 70-mark theory paper set by the school on the CBSE pattern. Cell: The Unit of Life opens Unit III, Cell: Structure and Function, which carries 15 marks shared with Biomolecules and Cell Cycle and Cell Division. In a typical school final this chapter alone is worth about 6 to 8 marks: one or two 1-mark MCQ or Assertion–Reason items, a 2-mark definition or difference, a 3-mark organelle question and, very commonly, a 5-mark question asking you to draw and describe a mitochondrion, chloroplast, nucleus or the fluid mosaic model. In NEET it is one of the most reliable chapters, with two to three questions almost every year taken word for word from NCERT.

question_types.note: Who discovered what (Hooke, Leeuwenhoek, Brown, Schleiden, Schwann, Virchow, Golgi, Palade, Singer and Nicolson); the odd one out among organelles (double membrane, single membrane, no membrane); 70S versus 80S ribosomes; the site of a process (rRNA synthesis in the nucleolus, lipid synthesis in SER, glycosylation in Golgi); the 9+2 versus 9+0 arrangement; the type of chromosome from centromere position; the smallest and largest cells.

Mitochondria and chloroplasts are semi-autonomous because they have their own DNA and 70S ribosomes; lysosomes are suicide bags; the plasma membrane is quasi-fluid; RER is abundant in secretory cells; the tonoplast moves ions against a gradient; prokaryotes lack membrane-bound organelles; mesosomes are extensions of the plasma membrane.

Define cell theory, mesosome, nucleoid, plasmid, glycocalyx, polysome, inclusion body, tonoplast, plasmodesmata, cristae, grana, axoneme, kinetochore, satellite; state two differences between RER and SER, cilia and flagella, 70S and 80S ribosomes, gram positive and gram negative bacteria.

Explain the fluid mosaic model; describe how substances cross the plasma membrane (passive, facilitated, active); functions of the Golgi apparatus; why lysosomes and vacuoles differ although both are endomembrane structures; classify chromosomes by centromere position with a diagram; characteristics of prokaryotic cells; components of the cell envelope; structure of the centriole.

Draw and describe the structure of a mitochondrion and a chloroplast; describe the nucleus with a labelled diagram; draw the ultrastructure of a bacterial cell; compare plant and animal cells with diagrams; describe the endomembrane system and the role of each component; describe the structure of cilia and flagella (axoneme) and centrioles.
A passage on a cell seen under the electron microscope, a secretory cell, a bacterium under Gram staining or a diseased cell whose lysosomes fail, followed by identify-and-justify sub-questions.

hot_topics: Mitochondria and chloroplast: structure, labelled diagram, semi-autonomy (own DNA, 70S ribosomes, division by fission)
Fluid mosaic model of the plasma membrane and transport across it (passive, facilitated, active, Na<sup>+</sup>/K<sup>+</sup> pump)
Nucleus and chromosomes: nuclear envelope, pores, nucleolus, chromatin, centromere-based types of chromosomes
Prokaryotic cell: cell envelope (glycocalyx, wall, membrane), gram staining, mesosome, plasmid, flagellum, pili, fimbriae, inclusion bodies, 70S ribosomes
Endomembrane system: RER versus SER, Golgi (cis and trans faces, glycosylation), lysosomes, vacuoles and the tonoplast
Cilia, flagella (9+2 axoneme) and centrioles (9 triplets, cartwheel, hub and spokes)
Cell theory: Schleiden, Schwann, Virchow and the discovery timeline (Hooke, Leeuwenhoek, Brown)
Differences: prokaryotic versus eukaryotic cell, plant versus animal cell, cell wall composition in plants, algae and fungi

sections.heading: 8.1 What is a Cell?
sections.body:
Every living organism is made of cells. Unicellular organisms such as Amoeba, Paramecium and bacteria carry out all life activities, including independent existence and reproduction, inside one cell. Multicellular organisms are built from many cells that divide the work among themselves. Anything less than a complete cell cannot live independently, which is why NCERT calls the cell the fundamental structural and functional unit of all living organisms. A cell separated from the body, with the right nutrients and conditions, can still perform metabolism and even divide; a nucleus or a mitochondrion taken out of a cell cannot.

The discovery came with the microscope. Anton von Leeuwenhoek was the first to see and describe a live cell. Robert Hooke observed a thin slice of cork and saw compartments, which he called cells. Robert Brown later discovered the nucleus (1831). The detailed structure of the cell that this chapter describes was revealed only after 1940, when the electron microscope made it possible to see the fine internal organisation that a light microscope cannot resolve. When a question asks why the cell was studied in such detail only in the twentieth century, this is the answer: the ultrastructure of organelles is beyond the resolving power of the light microscope.

The examiner's favourite two-mark question from this section is why the cell is the basic unit of life. Give three points: all organisms are made of cells and their products; the cell is the smallest unit that shows all the properties of life, such as metabolism, growth, response and reproduction; and in multicellular organisms the activities of the whole body are the sum of the activities of its cells, with the cells showing division of labour.
sections.tip: Do not mix up the credits: Leeuwenhoek saw a live cell first, Hooke saw dead cork cells and coined the word, Brown found the nucleus. The first NCERT exercise question is built exactly on this confusion.

sections.heading: 8.2 Cell Theory
sections.body:
In 1838 Matthias Schleiden, a German botanist, examined a large number of plants and observed that all plants are composed of different kinds of cells that form the tissues of the plant. In 1839 Theodore Schwann, a British zoologist, studied animal cells and reported that they have a thin outer layer, known today as the plasma membrane. From his study of plant tissues he also concluded that the cell wall is a unique feature of plant cells. On the basis of this Schwann proposed the hypothesis that the bodies of animals and plants are composed of cells and the products of cells.

Schleiden and Schwann together formulated the cell theory, but their theory did not explain how new cells are formed. Rudolf Virchow (1855) first explained that cells divide and new cells are formed from pre-existing cells, in his famous phrase Omnis cellula-e cellula. He modified the hypothesis of Schleiden and Schwann to give the cell theory its final shape.

The cell theory as it is understood today states two things, and the examiner wants both: (i) all living organisms are composed of cells and products of cells, and (ii) all cells arise from pre-existing cells. If you are asked for the contributions of the three scientists separately, write Schleiden for plants, Schwann for animals (plasma membrane, cell wall unique to plants) and Virchow for the origin of new cells from pre-existing cells. Exemplar questions also ask what was missing from the original theory; the answer is that it did not explain the origin of new cells, which Virchow supplied.

A quick check on the word 'products of cells': bone matrix, cartilage matrix, the cuticle of a leaf and the secondary cell wall are non-living products of cells, and the cell theory covers them through this phrase. Viruses do not fit the cell theory because they are acellular and cannot be called cells at all.
sections.tip: Write the Latin phrase correctly: Omnis cellula-e cellula, meaning all cells arise from pre-existing cells, credited to Virchow in 1855.

sections.heading: 8.3 An Overview of Cell
sections.body:
Under a microscope an onion peel shows plant cells and a human cheek scraping shows animal cells. Each cell has an outer cell membrane; plant cells have a rigid cell wall outside it as well. Inside is a dense, membrane-bound structure, the nucleus, which contains the chromosomes, which in turn contain the genetic material, DNA. The semi-fluid matrix filling the cell is the cytoplasm, the main arena of cellular activities in both plant and animal cells, where the chemical reactions that keep the cell alive take place.

Cells that have a membrane-bound nucleus are eukaryotic; cells that lack one are prokaryotic. Both types have the cytoplasm, but eukaryotic cells also have other membrane-bound distinct structures called organelles: endoplasmic reticulum, Golgi complex, lysosomes, mitochondria, microbodies and vacuoles. Prokaryotic cells lack such membrane-bound organelles. Ribosomes are non-membrane-bound organelles found in all cells, both eukaryotic and prokaryotic; in a eukaryotic cell they occur free in the cytoplasm, on the rough endoplasmic reticulum, and inside the chloroplasts and mitochondria. Animal cells contain a further non-membranous organelle, the centrosome, which helps in cell division.

Cells vary enormously in size, shape and activity. Mycoplasmas, the smallest cells, are only about 0.3 µm in length; bacteria may be 3 to 5 µm; the largest isolated single cell is the egg of an ostrich. Among multicellular organisms, human red blood cells are about 7.0 µm in diameter and nerve cells are among the longest cells. In shape cells may be disc-like (RBC), polygonal (many epithelial and plant cells), columnar (columnar epithelium), cuboid, thread-like (some fungal hyphae) or irregular (white blood cells, nerve cells with long processes). The exemplar asks you to arrange cells in increasing order of size; the order is Mycoplasma, bacteria, human RBC, ostrich egg.

formulas.expr: Mycoplasma ≈ 0.3 µm; bacteria 3–5 µm; human RBC ≈ 7.0 µm; ostrich egg = largest isolated single cell

sections.tip: Ribosomes and centrosome are the two organelles without a membrane. Ribosomes are in every cell; the centrosome is only in animal cells.

sections.heading: 8.4 Prokaryotic Cells: general organisation
sections.body:
Prokaryotic cells are represented by bacteria, blue-green algae (cyanobacteria), mycoplasma and PPLO (pleuro-pneumonia-like organisms). They are generally smaller than eukaryotic cells and multiply much faster. Bacteria come in four basic shapes: bacillus (rod-like), coccus (spherical), vibrio (comma-shaped) and spirillum (spiral).

The organisation of the prokaryotic cell is fundamentally similar in all of them, even though they vary greatly in shape and function. All have a cell wall surrounding the cell membrane, except in mycoplasma, which has no wall. The fluid matrix filling the cell is the cytoplasm. There is no well-defined nucleus. The genomic DNA, a single circular chromosome, is not enclosed by a nuclear membrane; NCERT says the genetic material is basically naked. In addition to the genomic DNA many bacteria have small circular DNA molecules outside the genomic DNA, called plasmids. Plasmids confer certain unique phenotypic characters on the bacterium, the most familiar being resistance to antibiotics. You meet plasmids again in Class 12 as the vectors of recombinant DNA technology; the same word is also used in the exemplar for extra-genomic DNA, along with the DNA of mitochondria and chloroplasts in eukaryotes.

Prokaryotes do not have membrane-bound organelles, but they do have a special membranous structure, the mesosome, formed by extensions of the plasma membrane into the cell in the form of vesicles, tubules and lamellae. Mesosomes help in cell wall formation, in DNA replication and its distribution to daughter cells, in respiration and secretion, and they increase the surface area of the plasma membrane and its enzymatic content. In some prokaryotes, such as cyanobacteria, there are other membranous extensions into the cytoplasm called chromatophores, which contain pigments.

Prokaryotes have ribosomes (70S) and reserve material stored as inclusion bodies, which are the subject of the next two sections. When a question asks for the characteristics of prokaryotic cells (NCERT exercise 8), list: small size and rapid multiplication; cell wall present (absent in mycoplasma); no nuclear membrane, naked circular genomic DNA; plasmids; no membrane-bound organelles; mesosomes; 70S ribosomes; inclusion bodies; flagella of a simple filament-hook-basal body type; pili and fimbriae.
sections.tip: Mycoplasma is the exception to remember twice: it is the smallest cell and it is the prokaryote without a cell wall.

sections.heading: 8.4.1 Cell Envelope and its Modifications
sections.body:
Most prokaryotic cells, particularly bacteria, have a chemically complex cell envelope. It consists of a tightly bound three-layered structure: the outermost glycocalyx, then the cell wall, and innermost the plasma membrane. Each layer performs a distinct function, but the three act together as a single protective unit.

Bacteria are classified into two groups on the basis of the differences in their cell envelopes and the way they respond to Gram staining, a procedure developed by Gram: those that take up the stain are gram positive and those that do not are gram negative. (The chemical basis, a thick peptidoglycan wall in gram positive bacteria and a thin wall with an outer membrane in gram negative bacteria, is not in NCERT but is worth one line if a 3-mark answer needs it.)

The glycocalyx differs in thickness and composition among bacteria. In some it is a loose sheath called the slime layer; in others it is thick and tough, called the capsule. The cell wall determines the shape of the cell and provides strong structural support to prevent the bacterium from bursting or collapsing. The plasma membrane is selectively permeable and interacts with the outside world; structurally it is similar to that of eukaryotes.

Bacterial cells may be motile or non-motile. If motile, they have thin filamentous extensions from the cell wall called flagella. Bacteria show a range in the number and arrangement of flagella. A bacterial flagellum has three parts: the filament, the hook and the basal body. The filament is the longest portion and extends from the cell surface to the outside. Note that the bacterial flagellum is structurally completely different from the eukaryotic flagellum: it has no 9+2 axoneme and is not covered by plasma membrane.

Besides flagella, pili and fimbriae are surface structures of bacteria that do not play a role in motility. Pili are elongated tubular structures made of a special protein. Fimbriae are small bristle-like fibres sprouting out of the cell; in some bacteria they are known to help attach the bacterium to rocks in streams and to host tissues.
sections.tip: A 2-mark favourite: distinguish flagella from pili and fimbriae. Flagella = motility, three parts (filament, hook, basal body); pili and fimbriae = attachment, no role in motility.

sections.heading: 8.4.2 Ribosomes and Inclusion Bodies
sections.body:
In prokaryotes the ribosomes are associated with the plasma membrane of the cell. They are about 15 nm by 20 nm in size and are made of two subunits, 50S and 30S, which together form a 70S ribosome. The letter S stands for the Svedberg unit or sedimentation coefficient, a measure of how fast a particle sediments in an ultracentrifuge; it depends on both size and density, which is why 50S + 30S gives 70S and not 80S. Ribosomes are the site of protein synthesis. Several ribosomes may attach to a single mRNA and form a chain called a polyribosome or polysome. The ribosomes of a polysome translate the mRNA into proteins, so many copies of the same polypeptide are made from one mRNA at the same time.

Inclusion bodies are the reserve material of prokaryotic cells stored in the cytoplasm. They are not bound by any membrane and lie free in the cytoplasm; this is the key phrase the marking scheme looks for. Examples are phosphate granules, cyanophycean granules and glycogen granules. Gas vacuoles are found in blue-green, purple and green photosynthetic bacteria; they are gas-filled structures that give buoyancy, keeping the cell at the depth of water where light and other conditions suit it.

Compare this with the eukaryotic cell while it is fresh in your mind: eukaryotic ribosomes are 80S (60S + 40S), but the ribosomes inside mitochondria and chloroplasts are the prokaryotic 70S type, which is one of the pieces of evidence that these organelles evolved from free-living prokaryotes (endosymbiosis). A question that asks for 'a feature common to prokaryotes and the mitochondria of eukaryotes' wants 70S ribosomes and circular naked DNA.

formulas.expr: Prokaryotic ribosome 70S = 50S + 30S; eukaryotic ribosome 80S = 60S + 40S; size ≈ 15 nm × 20 nm

sections.tip: Inclusion bodies are not membrane bound. If you write 'membrane-bound inclusion bodies' you lose the mark; the whole point is that prokaryotes have no membrane-bound organelles.

sections.heading: 8.5 Eukaryotic Cells and 8.5.1 Cell Membrane
sections.body:
Eukaryotes include all the protists, plants, animals and fungi. Their cells possess an organised nucleus with a nuclear envelope, and the cytoplasm is divided into compartments by an extensive endomembrane system. The genetic material is organised into chromosomes. Eukaryotic cells are not all identical: plant cells have cell walls, plastids and a large central vacuole, which animal cells lack; animal cells have centrioles, which are absent in almost all plant cells.

The detailed structure of the cell membrane was studied only after the advent of the electron microscope in the 1950s. Chemical studies, especially of the human erythrocyte (RBC) membrane, showed that it is composed of lipids arranged in a bilayer, with proteins. The lipids are mainly phosphoglycerides, and the membrane also contains cholesterol. In the erythrocyte membrane there is approximately 52 per cent protein and 40 per cent lipid. The lipid molecules are arranged with their polar heads towards the outer sides and the hydrophobic tails towards the inner part, so the non-polar tails are never exposed to the aqueous environment. The membrane proteins are of two kinds: integral proteins that are partially or totally buried in the membrane, and peripheral proteins that lie on the surface.

The fluid mosaic model, proposed by Singer and Nicolson in 1972, is the widely accepted model. According to it the quasi-fluid nature of the lipid bilayer enables the lateral movement of proteins within the bilayer; the proteins are like tiles in a mosaic floating in the lipid sea. The ability to move within the membrane is measured as its fluidity. This fluid nature is important for functions such as cell growth, formation of intercellular junctions, secretion, endocytosis and cell division.

The most important function of the plasma membrane is the transport of molecules across it. The membrane is selectively permeable. Some molecules move across it without any requirement of energy, which is passive transport: neutral solutes move by simple diffusion along the concentration gradient (high to low), and water moves by osmosis, also a passive process. Polar molecules cannot pass through the non-polar lipid bilayer, so they require a carrier protein to facilitate their transport across the membrane (facilitated diffusion, still passive). A few ions or molecules are transported against their concentration gradient, from lower to higher concentration; this is active transport, an energy-dependent process using ATP, such as the Na+/K+ pump. NCERT exercise 6 is exactly this paragraph and it is a standard 3-mark item.

formulas.expr: Erythrocyte membrane: ≈ 52% protein, 40% lipid; lipids = phosphoglycerides (+ cholesterol)

sections.tip: Three words the examiner underlines: quasi-fluid, lateral movement, selectively permeable. In the transport answer, separate passive (no energy, along the gradient) from active (ATP, against the gradient) and give the Na+/K+ pump as the example.

sections.heading: 8.5.2 Cell Wall
sections.body:
As Schwann pointed out, the cell wall is a feature of plant cells (and fungi), not animal cells. It is a non-living rigid structure outside the plasma membrane. It gives shape to the cell, protects it from mechanical damage and infection, helps in cell-to-cell interaction and provides a barrier to undesirable macromolecules.

The chemistry differs between groups, and this is asked as a 1-mark or 2-mark question. In algae the cell wall is made of cellulose, galactans, mannans and minerals like calcium carbonate. In other plants it consists of cellulose, hemicellulose, pectins and proteins. In fungi the wall is made of chitin, and in bacteria it is peptidoglycan (from Chapter 2, Biological Classification); the exemplar asks which of these is not true of eukaryotes, and the answer is a peptidoglycan wall.

The cell wall of a young plant cell, the primary wall, is capable of growth; it gradually diminishes as the cell matures, and the secondary wall is formed on the inner (inside) side of the cell, between the primary wall and the plasma membrane. The middle lamella is a layer mainly of calcium pectate that holds or glues the different neighbouring cells together. The cell wall and the middle lamella may be traversed by plasmodesmata, cytoplasmic strands that connect the cytoplasm of neighbouring cells so that materials can pass from cell to cell; this is how the symplast path of Chapter 11 works.

Do not describe the cell wall as 'selectively permeable'. It is freely permeable; selective permeability belongs to the plasma membrane. And never write cellulose for fungi or chitin for plants, a slip that costs the whole mark.
sections.tip: Middle lamella = calcium pectate; algae walls may contain calcium carbonate. Keep the two calcium compounds apart.

sections.heading: 8.5.3 Endomembrane System: Endoplasmic Reticulum and Golgi Apparatus
sections.body:
Each membranous organelle of the eukaryotic cell has its own structure and function, but the functions of some of them are coordinated, and these are considered together as the endomembrane system: the endoplasmic reticulum (ER), Golgi complex, lysosomes and vacuoles. Since the functions of the mitochondria, chloroplasts and peroxisomes are not coordinated with these, they are not considered part of the endomembrane system. The examiner often asks precisely this: name the components and state which organelles are excluded and why.

The endoplasmic reticulum is a network or reticulum of tiny tubular structures scattered in the cytoplasm. It divides the intracellular space into two distinct compartments: the luminal (inside the ER) and the extra-luminal (cytoplasm) compartments. When ribosomes are attached to the outer surface the ER is called rough endoplasmic reticulum (RER); in the absence of ribosomes it appears smooth and is called smooth endoplasmic reticulum (SER). RER is frequently observed in cells actively involved in protein synthesis and secretion; it is extensive and continuous with the outer membrane of the nucleus. SER is the major site for synthesis of lipids; in animal cells lipid-like steroidal hormones are synthesised in the SER. That is why the exemplar says RER is easily seen in secretory cells, and why liver cells and cells of the adrenal cortex and testis are rich in SER.

The Golgi apparatus was first observed by Camillo Golgi in 1898 as densely stained reticular structures near the nucleus. It consists of many flat, disc-shaped sacs or cisternae of 0.5 µm to 1.0 µm diameter, stacked parallel to each other. Varied numbers of cisternae are present in a Golgi complex. The cisternae are concentrically arranged near the nucleus with distinct convex cis (forming) and concave trans (maturing) faces; the two faces are entirely different but interconnected. The Golgi apparatus principally performs the function of packaging materials, to be delivered either to intracellular targets or secreted outside the cell. Materials to be packaged in the form of vesicles from the ER fuse with the cis face and move towards the maturing face. This explains why the Golgi apparatus remains in close association with the ER. A number of proteins synthesised by ribosomes on the ER are modified in the cisternae of the Golgi before release from the trans face. The Golgi apparatus is the important site of formation of glycoproteins and glycolipids (glycosylation).

formulas.expr: Golgi cisternae 0.5–1.0 µm; cis face = forming (convex, receives ER vesicles), trans face = maturing (concave, releases vesicles)

sections.tip: RER = protein synthesis and secretion, continuous with the nuclear envelope; SER = lipid and steroid hormone synthesis. Golgi = packaging + glycoproteins/glycolipids. The 3-mark 'functions of Golgi' answer must mention cis and trans faces.

sections.heading: 8.5.3 Endomembrane System: Lysosomes and Vacuoles
sections.body:
Lysosomes are membrane-bound vesicular structures formed by the process of packaging in the Golgi apparatus. The isolated lysosomal vesicles have been found to be very rich in almost all types of hydrolytic enzymes (hydrolases): lipases, proteases and carbohydrases, which are optimally active at acidic pH. These enzymes are capable of digesting carbohydrates, proteins, lipids and nucleic acids. Because they can digest the cell's own material when released, lysosomes are popularly called suicide bags of the cell (the phrase is from Class 9, but examiners still reward it). They also digest worn-out organelles and material brought in by endocytosis, and they play a role in the defence of white blood cells.

A vacuole is the membrane-bound space found in the cytoplasm. It contains water, sap, excretory products and other materials not useful for the cell. The vacuole is bound by a single membrane called the tonoplast. In plant cells the vacuoles can occupy up to 90 per cent of the volume of the cell. The tonoplast facilitates the transport of a number of ions and other materials against concentration gradients into the vacuole, so their concentration is significantly higher in the vacuole than in the cytoplasm; this is what maintains turgor. In Amoeba the contractile vacuole is important for excretion and osmoregulation. In many cells, as in protists, food vacuoles are formed by engulfing food particles.

NCERT exercise 12 asks you to comment on how lysosomes and vacuoles differ although both are endomembrane structures. Answer in a table: lysosomes are small vesicles formed from the Golgi, contain hydrolytic enzymes active at acidic pH, and digest macromolecules and worn-out organelles (intracellular digestion, defence, autolysis); vacuoles are larger single-membrane spaces bound by the tonoplast, contain water, sap and waste, store materials and ions moved in against a gradient, and maintain turgidity; in protists they act as contractile or food vacuoles.
sections.tip: Lysosomal enzymes work at acidic pH; that is the reason they do not digest the cytoplasm as long as the membrane is intact. Mention 'acidic pH' and 'hydrolases' for the enzyme mark.

sections.heading: 8.5.4 Mitochondria
sections.body:
Mitochondria, unless specifically stained, are not easily visible under the microscope; the vital stain for them is Janus green. The number of mitochondria per cell is variable and depends on the physiological activity of the cell; a muscle cell or a liver cell has many. In shape and size too they show considerable variation. Typically a mitochondrion is sausage-shaped or cylindrical, 0.2 to 1.0 µm in diameter (average 0.5 µm) and 1.0 to 4.1 µm in length.

Each mitochondrion is a double membrane-bound structure, with the outer membrane and the inner membrane dividing its lumen distinctly into two aqueous compartments: the outer compartment (intermembrane space) and the inner compartment. The inner compartment is called the matrix. The outer membrane forms the continuous limiting boundary of the organelle. The inner membrane forms a number of infoldings called cristae towards the matrix. The cristae increase the surface area; this is where the electron transport chain and ATP synthesis of Chapter 12 (Respiration in Plants) sit. The two membranes have their own specific enzymes associated with mitochondrial function.

Mitochondria are the sites of aerobic respiration. They produce cellular energy in the form of ATP, hence they are called the power houses of the cell. The matrix also possesses a single circular DNA molecule, a few RNA molecules, ribosomes (70S) and the components required for the synthesis of proteins. Mitochondria divide by fission. Because they have their own DNA, ribosomes and protein-synthesising machinery and divide independently, mitochondria (and chloroplasts) are called semi-autonomous organelles; they are not fully autonomous because most of their proteins are coded by nuclear genes.

For the 5-mark version of NCERT exercise 7, draw the mitochondrion and the chloroplast side by side (see the diagrams section), list the shared characteristics (double membrane, own circular DNA, 70S ribosomes, division by fission, semi-autonomy) and then give each organelle's function.

formulas.expr: Mitochondrion: length 1.0–4.1 µm, diameter 0.2–1.0 µm (average 0.5 µm); double membrane; inner folds = cristae; matrix has circular DNA + 70S ribosomes

sections.tip: Cristae are folds of the inner membrane, never the outer. NCERT exercise 3 matches cristae with 'infoldings in mitochondria'; get the match table right: cristae–mitochondria, cisternae–Golgi, thylakoids–stroma of chloroplast.

sections.heading: 8.5.5 Plastids
sections.body:
Plastids are found in all plant cells and in euglenoids. They are easily observed under the microscope because they are large. They bear specific pigments, which impart specific colours to the plants. Based on the pigments they contain, plastids are of three types.

Chloroplasts contain chlorophyll and carotenoid pigments, which are responsible for trapping light energy for photosynthesis. Chromoplasts contain fat-soluble carotenoid pigments such as carotene and xanthophylls, giving the part of the plant a yellow, orange or red colour (the ripe tomato, the carrot root). Leucoplasts are colourless plastids of varied shapes and sizes that store nutrients: amyloplasts store carbohydrates (starch, as in the potato tuber), elaioplasts store oils and fats, and aleuroplasts store proteins. The exemplar asks whether plastids are interchangeable, and the answer is yes: chloroplasts turn into chromoplasts when a tomato ripens, and the leucoplasts of a potato tuber turn green (chloroplasts) when exposed to light.

Chloroplasts of the majority of green plants are found in the mesophyll cells of leaves. They are lens-shaped, oval, spherical, discoid or even ribbon-like organelles, 5 to 10 µm in length and 2 to 4 µm in width. Their number varies from one per cell in the green alga Chlamydomonas to 20 to 40 per cell in the mesophyll. Like mitochondria, chloroplasts are double membrane-bound; of the two, the inner membrane is relatively less permeable. The space limited by the inner membrane is the stroma. A number of organised flattened membranous sacs called thylakoids are present in the stroma. Thylakoids are arranged in stacks like piles of coins called grana (singular granum), and there are about 40 to 60 grana per chloroplast. Flat membranous tubules called stroma lamellae connect the thylakoids of different grana. The membrane of the thylakoids encloses a space called the lumen. The stroma contains the enzymes required for the synthesis of carbohydrates and proteins (the Calvin cycle of Chapter 11), a double-stranded circular DNA and 70S ribosomes. The chlorophyll pigments are present in the thylakoid membranes.

The difference the exemplar tests: plastids differ from mitochondria in having thylakoids (and pigments). Everything else on the list, double membrane, own DNA, 70S ribosomes, is shared.

formulas.expr: Chloroplast: 5–10 µm × 2–4 µm; 1 per cell (Chlamydomonas) to 20–40 per mesophyll cell; 40–60 grana per chloroplast
where: flattened sac; stacks = grana; connections = stroma lamellae; inside = lumen

sections.tip: Stroma is the matrix inside the inner membrane; stroma lamellae are the tubules connecting grana. In the diagram both must be labelled separately.

sections.heading: 8.5.6 Ribosomes and 8.5.7 Cytoskeleton
sections.body:
Ribosomes were first observed under the electron microscope as dense particles by George Palade (1953). They are granular structures composed of ribonucleic acid (RNA) and proteins, and they are not surrounded by any membrane. The eukaryotic ribosomes are 80S, made of two subunits, 60S and 40S; the prokaryotic ribosomes are 70S (50S + 30S). Here S denotes the sedimentation coefficient, which is indirectly a measure of density and size, so the values of the subunits are not additive. Ribosomes are the site of protein synthesis in every cell. In eukaryotes they occur free in the cytoplasm, bound to the RER, and inside mitochondria and chloroplasts (where they are 70S). Several ribosomes on one mRNA form a polysome, as in prokaryotes.

The cytoskeleton is an elaborate network of filamentous proteinaceous structures present in the cytoplasm: microtubules (tubulin), microfilaments (actin) and intermediate filaments. NCERT gives its functions in one line, and you should give all three: mechanical support, motility, and maintenance of the shape of the cell. Microtubules also build the spindle, the axoneme of cilia and flagella and the centrioles, which is why the next section follows.

The exemplar asks which is not a function of the cytoskeleton and the trick is that all the listed functions (intracellular transport, support, shape, motility) are genuine. It also asks what is common to ribosomes and centrioles; the answer is that neither has a membrane.

formulas.expr: Eukaryotic ribosome 80S = 60S + 40S; discovered by George Palade (1953); RNA + protein; no membrane

sections.tip: If a question says 'ribosomes have no role in protein synthesis' or 'ribosomes are membrane bound', it is the false option.

sections.heading: 8.5.8 Cilia and Flagella, 8.5.9 Centrosome and Centrioles
sections.body:
Cilia (singular cilium) and flagella (singular flagellum) are hair-like outgrowths of the cell membrane. Cilia are small structures that work like oars, causing the movement of either the cell or the surrounding fluid (the ciliated epithelium of the trachea moves mucus; Paramecium swims with cilia). Flagella are comparatively longer and responsible for cell movement (sperm, Euglena). The prokaryotic bacteria also possess flagella, but these are structurally different from the eukaryotic flagella.

The electron microscope shows that a cilium or flagellum is covered with plasma membrane. Their core, called the axoneme, possesses a number of microtubules running parallel to the long axis. The axoneme usually has nine doublets of radially arranged peripheral microtubules and a pair of centrally located microtubules. This arrangement of the axonemal microtubules is referred to as the 9+2 array. The central tubules are connected by bridges and are also enclosed by a central sheath, which is connected to one of the tubules of each peripheral doublet by a radial spoke; thus there are nine radial spokes. The peripheral doublets are also interconnected by linkers (interdoublet linkers). Both the cilium and the flagellum emerge from centriole-like structures called basal bodies.

The centrosome is an organelle usually containing two cylindrical structures called centrioles, surrounded by amorphous pericentriolar material. Both the centrioles in a centrosome lie perpendicular to each other, and each has an organisation like a cartwheel. They are made up of nine evenly spaced peripheral fibrils of tubulin protein. Each of the peripheral fibrils is a triplet, and the adjacent triplets are also linked. The central part of the proximal region of the centriole is also proteinaceous and is called the hub, which is connected with the tubules of the peripheral triplets by radial spokes made of protein. There are no central microtubules, so the arrangement is described as 9+0 with triplets. The centrioles form the basal body of cilia or flagella and the spindle fibres that give rise to the spindle apparatus during cell division in animal cells. Note the contrast that the examiner loves: axoneme = 9 doublets + 2 central singlets, covered by plasma membrane; centriole = 9 triplets + 0 central, hub and spokes, no membrane.

formulas.expr: Axoneme: 9 peripheral doublets + 2 central singlets (9+2), 9 radial spokes, central sheath, interdoublet linkers; Centriole: 9 peripheral triplets + 0 (9+0), hub and radial spokes, cartwheel
where: centriole-like structure from which a cilium or flagellum arises

sections.tip: Write 'doublets' for the axoneme and 'triplets' for the centriole. Swapping them is the most common loss of marks in this section.

sections.heading: 8.5.10 Nucleus and chromosomes
sections.body:
The nucleus, as a cell organelle, was first described by Robert Brown in 1831. Later the material of the nucleus stained by basic dyes was given the name chromatin by Flemming. The interphase nucleus (the nucleus of a cell when it is not dividing) has highly extended and elaborate nucleoprotein fibres called chromatin, a nuclear matrix, and one or more spherical bodies called nucleoli (singular nucleolus).

Electron microscopy shows that the nuclear envelope consists of two parallel membranes with a space between them (10 to 50 nm) called the perinuclear space; it forms a barrier between the materials present inside the nucleus and the cytoplasm. The outer membrane usually remains continuous with the endoplasmic reticulum and also bears ribosomes on it. At a number of places the nuclear envelope is interrupted by minute pores, formed by the fusion of its two membranes; these nuclear pores are the passages through which the movement of RNA and protein molecules takes place in both directions between the nucleus and the cytoplasm (NCERT exercise 11). Normally there is only one nucleus per cell, but variations are found: some mature cells lack a nucleus altogether, such as the erythrocytes of many mammals and the sieve tube cells of vascular plants (the exemplar's 'common feature'), although they had one during development.

The nucleoplasm contains the nucleolus and chromatin. The nucleoli are spherical structures present in the nucleoplasm, and their content is continuous with the rest of the nucleoplasm because they are not membrane-bound. The nucleolus is the site of active ribosomal RNA synthesis, so larger and more numerous nucleoli are present in cells actively carrying out protein synthesis.

During different stages of cell division cells show structured chromosomes in place of the nucleus. Chromatin contains DNA and some basic proteins called histones, some non-histone proteins and also RNA. A single human cell has approximately two metres long thread of DNA distributed among its forty-six (twenty-three pairs) chromosomes. Every chromosome, visible only in dividing cells, essentially has a primary constriction or the centromere, on the sides of which disc-shaped structures called kinetochores are present (where spindle fibres attach). Based on the position of the centromere, chromosomes are of four types. The metacentric chromosome has a middle centromere forming two equal arms. In the sub-metacentric chromosome the centromere is slightly away from the middle, resulting in one shorter arm and one longer arm. In the acrocentric chromosome the centromere is situated close to its end, forming one extremely short and one very long arm. The telocentric chromosome has a terminal centromere. Besides the primary constriction a few chromosomes have non-staining secondary constrictions at a constant location, which give the appearance of a small fragment called the satellite (a satellite chromosome; the exemplar calls it a marker chromosome).

formulas.expr: Nuclear envelope: 2 membranes, perinuclear space 10–50 nm, outer membrane continuous with ER and bears ribosomes; nuclear pores pass RNA and proteins; human cell ≈ 2 m DNA in 46 chromosomes
where: metacentric, sub-metacentric, acrocentric, telocentric (by centromere position)

sections.tip: For the chromosome-type diagram draw four chromosomes with the centromere moving from the middle to the tip, label each arm length, and write 'kinetochore' on the centromere. Exercise 14 is asked almost every year.

sections.heading: 8.5.11 Microbodies, and the two comparisons every paper asks
sections.body:
Microbodies are many membrane-bound minute vesicles that contain various enzymes; they are present in both plant and animal cells. NCERT gives only this one line. The peroxisomes (which contain catalase and break down hydrogen peroxide, and take part in photorespiration in leaves) and glyoxysomes (in germinating fatty seeds) are the well-known examples, and a line on them earns credit in a 3-mark answer on organelles that are not part of the endomembrane system.

Prokaryotic versus eukaryotic cell. Size: prokaryotes generally smaller (1 to 10 µm), eukaryotes larger (10 to 100 µm). Nucleus: absent, naked circular DNA in the cytoplasm versus a true nucleus with a nuclear envelope, nucleolus and linear chromosomes with histones. Membrane-bound organelles: absent (mesosomes and chromatophores only) versus present (ER, Golgi, lysosomes, mitochondria, plastids, vacuoles, microbodies). Ribosomes: 70S versus 80S in the cytoplasm. Cell wall: peptidoglycan versus cellulose (plants) or chitin (fungi) or absent (animals). Flagella: filament, hook, basal body versus 9+2 axoneme covered by plasma membrane. Cell division: fission versus mitosis and meiosis. Examples: bacteria, cyanobacteria, mycoplasma, PPLO versus protists, fungi, plants, animals.

Plant cell versus animal cell. Cell wall of cellulose present in plants, absent in animals. Plastids present in plants, absent in animals. Vacuole: a large central vacuole occupying up to 90 per cent of the volume in plants; small, few or absent in animals. Centrioles: absent in most plants, present in animals. Lysosomes: rare in plants, common in animals. Shape: fixed (polygonal or rectangular) in plants because of the wall, variable in animals. Storage material: starch in plants, glycogen in animals. Plasmodesmata in plants; none in animals. Write these as a table with two columns; five differences are enough for a 3-mark question and eight for 5 marks with diagrams.
sections.tip: In any 'difference' table, name the feature in the first column (cell wall, plastids, vacuole, centrioles, lysosomes) and put one word or phrase in each of the other two. Long sentences in tables get no extra credit.

key_terms.definition: All living organisms are composed of cells and products of cells, and all cells arise from pre-existing cells (Schleiden and Schwann, 1838–39; Virchow, 1855).
Virchow's statement (1855) that new cells arise only from pre-existing cells by division.
A cell lacking a membrane-bound nucleus and membrane-bound organelles, with naked circular genomic DNA and 70S ribosomes; bacteria, cyanobacteria, mycoplasma, PPLO.
A cell with a true nucleus bounded by a nuclear envelope and an extensive endomembrane system; protists, fungi, plants and animals.
The region of a prokaryotic cell where the naked circular genomic DNA lies, not enclosed by any membrane.
Small circular DNA outside the genomic DNA in bacteria that confers phenotypic characters such as antibiotic resistance; used as a vector in genetic engineering.

Extension of the plasma membrane of a prokaryote into the cell as vesicles, tubules and lamellae; helps in cell wall formation, DNA replication and distribution, respiration and secretion, and increases membrane surface area and enzyme content.
Pigment-containing membranous extension into the cytoplasm found in some prokaryotes such as cyanobacteria.
The three-layered outer covering of a bacterial cell: glycocalyx (slime layer or capsule), cell wall and plasma membrane, acting together as a protective unit.
Outermost layer of the bacterial envelope; a loose sheath is called a slime layer and a thick, tough layer a capsule.
Staining procedure developed by Gram; bacteria that take up the stain are gram positive, those that do not are gram negative.
Bacterial surface structures with no role in motility: pili are elongated tubular protein structures; fimbriae are small bristle-like fibres that help attach the bacterium to rocks or host tissues.
A chain of several ribosomes attached to a single mRNA, translating it simultaneously into many copies of the same protein.
Reserve material of prokaryotes stored free in the cytoplasm without any membrane: phosphate granules, cyanophycean granules, glycogen granules, gas vacuoles.
Singer and Nicolson's 1972 model of the plasma membrane: a quasi-fluid phospholipid bilayer in which proteins (integral and peripheral) are embedded and can move laterally.
Energy (ATP) dependent movement of ions or molecules across the membrane against their concentration gradient, e.g. the Na<sup>+</sup>/K<sup>+</sup> pump.
Layer of calcium pectate between adjacent plant cells that glues the neighbouring cells together.
Cytoplasmic strands passing through the cell wall and middle lamella that connect the cytoplasm of neighbouring plant cells.
The set of organelles whose functions are coordinated: endoplasmic reticulum, Golgi complex, lysosomes and vacuoles. Mitochondria, chloroplasts and peroxisomes are excluded.
Flat, disc-shaped sacs of 0.5–1.0 µm diameter stacked parallel to each other in the Golgi apparatus, with a cis (forming) and a trans (maturing) face.
Membrane-bound vesicle formed by packaging in the Golgi apparatus, rich in hydrolytic enzymes (lipases, proteases, carbohydrases) active at acidic pH.
The single membrane bounding the plant cell vacuole; it transports ions and other materials into the vacuole against concentration gradients.
Infoldings of the inner mitochondrial membrane towards the matrix that increase the surface area for the enzymes of aerobic respiration.
Mitochondria and chloroplasts, which have their own circular DNA, RNA and 70S ribosomes and divide by fission, but still depend on nuclear genes for most of their proteins.
Grana are stacks of thylakoids (40–60 per chloroplast) in the stroma; stroma lamellae are flat membranous tubules connecting the thylakoids of different grana.
Colourless plastid that stores nutrients: amyloplasts (starch), elaioplasts (oils and fats), aleuroplasts (proteins).
The microtubular core of a cilium or flagellum: nine peripheral doublets and two central singlet microtubules (9+2), with a central sheath, nine radial spokes and interdoublet linkers.

Cylindrical structure of the centrosome with a cartwheel organisation of nine peripheral triplet fibrils of tubulin, a central proteinaceous hub and radial spokes; forms basal bodies and spindle fibres.
The 10–50 nm space between the two membranes of the nuclear envelope.
Non-membrane-bound spherical body in the nucleoplasm that is the site of active ribosomal RNA synthesis.
Nucleoprotein fibres of the interphase nucleus made of DNA, basic histone proteins, non-histone proteins and RNA; named by Flemming.
The centromere is the primary constriction of a chromosome; kinetochores are the disc-shaped structures on its sides to which spindle fibres attach.
A chromosome with a non-staining secondary constriction at a constant location, giving the appearance of a small fragment called the satellite.
Membrane-bound minute vesicles containing various enzymes, present in both plant and animal cells; peroxisomes are the common example.

formula_sheet.name: Discovery timeline
formula_sheet.expr: Leeuwenhoek: first saw a live cell; Hooke: cork 'cells'; Brown: nucleus (1831); Schleiden (1838) and Schwann (1839): cell theory; Virchow (1855): Omnis cellula-e cellula; Golgi (1898): Golgi apparatus; Palade (1953): ribosomes; Singer and Nicolson (1972): fluid mosaic model; Flemming: chromatin
formula_sheet.note: The first MCQ in almost every paper is one of these credits.

formula_sheet.name: Cell sizes
formula_sheet.expr: Mycoplasma 0.3 µm (smallest) < bacteria 3–5 µm < human RBC 7.0 µm < ostrich egg (largest isolated single cell); nerve cells the longest

formula_sheet.name: Ribosomes
formula_sheet.expr: Prokaryote 70S = 50S + 30S (15 nm × 20 nm); eukaryote 80S = 60S + 40S; mitochondria and chloroplasts 70S; S = Svedberg (sedimentation coefficient), not additive
formula_sheet.note: No membrane; RNA + protein; polysome = many ribosomes on one mRNA.

formula_sheet.name: Plasma membrane composition
formula_sheet.expr: Erythrocyte membrane ≈ 52% protein + 40% lipid; lipids = phosphoglycerides (+ cholesterol); proteins integral and peripheral
formula_sheet.note: Polar heads outside, hydrophobic tails inside; quasi-fluid; lateral movement of proteins.

formula_sheet.name: Transport across the membrane
formula_sheet.expr: Passive: simple diffusion (neutral solutes), osmosis (water), facilitated diffusion via carrier proteins (polar molecules); Active: against the gradient using ATP, e.g. Na<sup>+</sup>/K<sup>+</sup> pump

formula_sheet.name: Cell wall chemistry
formula_sheet.expr: Algae: cellulose, galactans, mannans, CaCO<sub>3</sub>; plants: cellulose, hemicellulose, pectins, proteins; fungi: chitin; bacteria: peptidoglycan; middle lamella: calcium pectate
formula_sheet.note: Primary wall grows and thins; secondary wall laid inside it; plasmodesmata cross both.

formula_sheet.name: Endomembrane system
formula_sheet.expr: ER (RER: protein synthesis and secretion, continuous with nuclear envelope; SER: lipids, steroid hormones) → Golgi (cis face receives, trans face releases; packaging; glycoproteins and glycolipids) → lysosomes (hydrolases, acidic pH) and vacuoles (tonoplast, up to 90% of plant cell volume)
formula_sheet.note: Mitochondria, chloroplasts and peroxisomes are NOT part of it.

formula_sheet.name: Mitochondrion numbers
formula_sheet.expr: Sausage-shaped; 1.0–4.1 µm long, 0.2–1.0 µm (avg 0.5 µm) wide; outer membrane smooth, inner folded into cristae; matrix = circular DNA + RNA + 70S ribosomes; divides by fission
formula_sheet.note: Power house: aerobic respiration, ATP. Stain: Janus green.

formula_sheet.name: Chloroplast numbers
formula_sheet.expr: 5–10 µm × 2–4 µm; 1 per cell (Chlamydomonas) to 20–40 per mesophyll cell; 40–60 grana per chloroplast; inner membrane less permeable; stroma has enzymes, circular ds DNA, 70S ribosomes; chlorophyll in thylakoid membranes
formula_sheet.note: Thylakoid stacks = grana; connecting tubules = stroma lamellae; thylakoid interior = lumen.

formula_sheet.name: Three kinds of plastids
formula_sheet.expr: Chloroplasts (chlorophyll + carotenoids); chromoplasts (carotene, xanthophylls: yellow, orange, red); leucoplasts (amyloplasts starch, elaioplasts oils, aleuroplasts proteins)
formula_sheet.note: Found in plant cells and euglenoids; interchangeable (tomato ripening, potato greening).

formula_sheet.name: Axoneme versus centriole
formula_sheet.expr: Cilium/flagellum: plasma membrane cover, 9 doublets + 2 central singlets, central sheath, 9 radial spokes, interdoublet linkers, basal body; Centriole: 9 triplets + 0, hub + radial spokes (cartwheel), two centrioles at right angles in pericentriolar material
formula_sheet.note: Bacterial flagellum is different: filament, hook, basal body.

formula_sheet.name: Nucleus numbers
formula_sheet.expr: Two membranes, perinuclear space 10–50 nm; outer membrane continuous with ER, bears ribosomes; nuclear pores pass RNA and proteins; nucleolus = rRNA synthesis, no membrane; human cell ≈ 2 m DNA in 46 chromosomes
formula_sheet.note: Enucleate cells: mammalian RBC, mature sieve tube cells.

formula_sheet.name: Chromosome types by centromere
formula_sheet.expr: Metacentric (middle, equal arms); sub-metacentric (slightly off-centre, one shorter and one longer arm); acrocentric (near the end, one very short arm); telocentric (terminal)
formula_sheet.note: Kinetochores on the centromere; secondary constriction gives a satellite.

formula_sheet.name: Membrane count of organelles
formula_sheet.expr: Double: mitochondria, chloroplasts, nucleus; Single: ER, Golgi, lysosomes, vacuoles, microbodies; None: ribosomes, centrioles, cytoskeleton, nucleolus
formula_sheet.note: Standard MCQ and exemplar LA classification.

diagrams.title: A typical bacterial cell (NCERT Figure 8.2)
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw a rod-shaped outline with three concentric layers on the outside: a faint outer halo (capsule or slime layer), a thick line (cell wall) and a thin inner line (plasma membrane). Inside, draw an irregular coiled thread in the centre (nucleoid, genomic DNA), one or two small circles (plasmids), many dots (ribosomes), a few larger granules (inclusion bodies), and one or two infoldings of the plasma membrane into the cytoplasm (mesosome). From one end draw a long wavy flagellum with a short bent hook and a basal body in the envelope; around the surface draw short bristles (fimbriae) and one or two longer tubes (pili). Label: capsule/glycocalyx, cell wall, plasma membrane, cytoplasm, nucleoid, plasmid, ribosomes, inclusion body, mesosome, flagellum (filament, hook, basal body), pili, fimbriae.

diagrams.title: Plant cell and animal cell (NCERT Figures 8.3 and 8.4), side by side
diagrams.how_to_draw: Plant cell: a rectangular outline with a thick double line (cell wall) and a thin line inside it (plasma membrane); a very large central vacuole bounded by the tonoplast pushing the nucleus to one side; nucleus with nuclear envelope, nucleolus and chromatin; several lens-shaped chloroplasts with stacked lines inside; a few mitochondria with cristae; RER with dots and SER as smooth tubules; a stack of Golgi cisternae; dots for ribosomes; tiny channels through the wall labelled plasmodesmata. Animal cell: a rounded, irregular outline with only the plasma membrane; central nucleus; mitochondria; RER and SER; Golgi; several small lysosomes; two short cylinders at right angles near the nucleus (centrioles in the centrosome); small vacuoles; ribosomes. Label at least eight parts on each and write beneath: plant cell has cell wall, plastids, large central vacuole, plasmodesmata; animal cell has centrioles and lysosomes.

diagrams.title: Fluid mosaic model of the plasma membrane (NCERT Figure 8.5)
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw two rows of phospholipid molecules, each as a small circle (polar head) with two wavy lines (non-polar tails), the heads facing outward on both surfaces and the tails meeting in the middle. Embed large blobs spanning the whole bilayer (integral proteins), one of them with a channel through it, and smaller blobs sitting only on a surface (peripheral proteins). On the outer surface attach short branched chains to some proteins and lipids (carbohydrate chains of glycoproteins and glycolipids). Add a few cholesterol molecules between the tails. Label: phospholipid bilayer, polar (hydrophilic) head, non-polar (hydrophobic) tail, integral protein, peripheral protein, carbohydrate, cholesterol, outer surface, inner surface. Write 'Singer and Nicolson, 1972' beside the title.

diagrams.title: Endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi apparatus (NCERT Figures 8.6 and 8.7)
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw part of the nuclear envelope at one edge and from its outer membrane draw a network of flattened sacs and tubules; dot the surface of the sacs near the nucleus (RER) and leave the tubules towards the periphery smooth (SER). Label: nuclear envelope, rough endoplasmic reticulum, ribosomes, smooth endoplasmic reticulum, lumen (luminal compartment), cytoplasm (extra-luminal compartment). Next to it draw a stack of five or six curved flattened sacs with swollen ends, the convex side facing the ER and the concave side facing away, small vesicles arriving on the convex side and leaving from the concave side. Label: cisternae, cis face (forming face), trans face (maturing face), transport vesicles from ER, secretory vesicles, lysosome budding from the trans face.

diagrams.title: Structure of a mitochondrion (NCERT Figure 8.8), longitudinal section
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw a sausage shape with two parallel outlines close together (outer membrane and inner membrane) and a small gap between them. Fold the inner line inward at several places into shelf-like plates that project into the interior (cristae). Fill the interior with light stippling (matrix), a small circle of thread (circular DNA) and dots (70S ribosomes). Label: outer membrane, inner membrane, outer compartment (intermembrane space), inner compartment (matrix), cristae, DNA, ribosomes. Write beneath: 1.0–4.1 µm long, 0.2–1.0 µm wide, site of aerobic respiration.

diagrams.title: Structure of a chloroplast (NCERT Figure 8.9), sectional view
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw a lens-shaped outline with two close parallel lines (outer membrane and inner membrane). Inside, draw four or five stacks of small flattened discs like piles of coins (grana, each disc a thylakoid) and connect neighbouring stacks with thin tubules (stroma lamellae). Fill the rest with light stippling (stroma), add a small ring of DNA and dots for ribosomes. Label: outer membrane, inner membrane, stroma, granum, thylakoid, stroma lamella, lumen of thylakoid, DNA, ribosome. Write beneath: 5–10 µm × 2–4 µm, 40–60 grana per chloroplast, chlorophyll in thylakoid membranes.

diagrams.title: Transverse section of a cilium or flagellum, the axoneme (NCERT Figure 8.10)
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw a circle for the plasma membrane. Just inside it draw nine pairs of small touching circles arranged evenly around the ring (peripheral doublets), and two separate circles at the centre (central singlet microtubules) with a short line joining them (bridge) and a ring around them (central sheath). From the central sheath draw nine lines outward, each to one microtubule of a doublet (radial spokes), and short connecting lines between neighbouring doublets (interdoublet linkers). Label: plasma membrane, peripheral doublet microtubules, central microtubules, bridge, central sheath, radial spoke, interdoublet linker, and write '9+2 arrangement'. Below, draw a longitudinal view showing the cilium arising from a basal body in the cytoplasm.

diagrams.title: Transverse section of a centriole (NCERT Figure 8.10 inset)
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw a circle without any membrane. Around it place nine evenly spaced groups of three small touching circles arranged like blades of a fan (peripheral triplet fibrils), link adjacent triplets with short lines, draw a small circle in the centre (hub) and nine lines from the hub to the innermost tubule of each triplet (radial spokes), giving a cartwheel. Label: triplet fibril (A, B, C tubules), hub, radial spoke, linker between triplets, and write '9+0 with triplets, tubulin protein'. Beside it, sketch the centrosome as two such cylinders at right angles inside a shaded cloud labelled pericentriolar material.

diagrams.title: Structure of the nucleus (NCERT Figure 8.11)
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw a large circle with a double outline (outer and inner nuclear membrane) with a narrow space between them; break the double line at three or four places where the two membranes join (nuclear pores). Continue the outer membrane at one place into a sheet with dots on it (RER continuous with the outer membrane, ribosomes on the outer membrane). Inside draw a dense round body (nucleolus) and a tangle of fine threads (chromatin) in a stippled ground (nucleoplasm). Label: nuclear envelope (outer membrane, inner membrane), perinuclear space, nuclear pore, nucleoplasm, nucleolus, chromatin, ribosomes, endoplasmic reticulum.

diagrams.title: Types of chromosomes based on the position of the centromere (NCERT Figure 8.12)
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw four chromosomes as pairs of rods (two chromatids) joined at a pinched point. First: centromere exactly in the middle, arms equal (metacentric). Second: centromere a little above the middle, one arm shorter (sub-metacentric). Third: centromere near one end, one arm very short (acrocentric). Fourth: centromere at the very tip (telocentric). Mark the centromere as the primary constriction and draw small discs on both sides of it labelled kinetochore. On one chromosome add a small knob separated by a narrow neck near the tip and label it secondary constriction and satellite. Label each chromosome type and write 'short arm (p)' and 'long arm (q)' on the sub-metacentric one.

ncert_questions.q: Which of the following is not correct? (a) Robert Brown discovered the cell. (b) Schleiden and Schwann formulated the cell theory. (c) Virchow explained that cells are formed from pre-existing cells. (d) A unicellular organism carries out its life activities within a single cell.
ncert_questions.a: (a) is not correct. Robert Brown discovered the nucleus (1831), not the cell. The cell was first seen and described alive by Anton von Leeuwenhoek, and Robert Hooke observed dead cork cells and coined the term. Statements (b), (c) and (d) are all correct.

ncert_questions.q: New cells generate from (a) bacterial fermentation (b) regeneration of old cells (c) pre-existing cells (d) abiotic materials.
ncert_questions.a: (c) pre-existing cells. This is Virchow's contribution to the cell theory: Omnis cellula-e cellula, all cells arise from pre-existing cells by division. Cells are never formed de novo from abiotic materials.

ncert_questions.q: Match the following: (a) Cristae (b) Cisternae (c) Thylakoids with (i) Flat membranous sacs in stroma (ii) Infoldings in mitochondria (iii) Disc-shaped sacs in Golgi apparatus.
ncert_questions.a:
(a) Cristae – (ii) Infoldings in mitochondria (folds of the inner membrane that increase surface area).
(b) Cisternae – (iii) Disc-shaped sacs in Golgi apparatus (0.5–1.0 µm, stacked parallel, cis and trans faces).
(c) Thylakoids – (i) Flat membranous sacs in stroma (stacked as grana in the chloroplast).

ncert_questions.q: Which of the following is correct: (a) Cells of all living organisms have a nucleus. (b) Both animal and plant cells have a well defined cell wall. (c) In prokaryotes, there are no membrane bound organelles. (d) Cells are formed de novo from abiotic materials.
ncert_questions.a: (c) is correct. Prokaryotic cells have no membrane-bound organelles; they have only mesosomes and chromatophores, which are extensions of the plasma membrane, and non-membranous ribosomes and inclusion bodies. (a) is wrong because prokaryotes lack a nucleus and mammalian RBCs and sieve tube cells lose theirs; (b) is wrong because animal cells have no cell wall; (d) contradicts the cell theory.

ncert_questions.q: What is a mesosome in a prokaryotic cell? Mention the functions that it performs.
ncert_questions.a:
A mesosome is a special membranous structure of a prokaryotic cell formed by the extension of the plasma membrane into the cell in the form of vesicles, tubules and lamellae.

Functions: (i) helps in cell wall formation; (ii) helps in DNA replication and the distribution of DNA to the daughter cells; (iii) helps in respiration (it carries respiratory enzymes) and secretion processes; (iv) increases the surface area of the plasma membrane and its enzymatic content.

ncert_questions.q: How do neutral solutes move across the plasma membrane? Can the polar molecules also move across it in the same way? If not, then how are these transported across the membrane?
ncert_questions.a:
Neutral solutes move across the plasma membrane by simple diffusion along the concentration gradient, from higher to lower concentration, without any expenditure of energy (passive transport). Water also moves passively, by osmosis.

Polar molecules cannot move across the membrane in the same way, because the interior of the lipid bilayer is non-polar (hydrophobic) and does not allow polar substances to pass through it.

Polar molecules are therefore transported with the help of carrier proteins present in the membrane (facilitated diffusion, still passive and along the gradient). Some ions and molecules are moved against their concentration gradient, from lower to higher concentration, by active transport, which requires energy in the form of ATP, for example the Na+/K+ pump.

ncert_questions.q: Name two cell-organelles that are double membrane bound. What are the characteristics of these two organelles? State their functions and draw labelled diagrams of both.
ncert_questions.a:
The two double-membrane-bound organelles are the mitochondrion and the chloroplast (the nucleus is also double-membraned).

Mitochondrion: sausage-shaped or cylindrical, 1.0–4.1 µm long and 0.2–1.0 µm wide. The outer membrane forms the continuous limiting boundary; the inner membrane is folded into cristae that increase the surface area. The two membranes divide the lumen into the outer compartment and the inner compartment or matrix. The matrix contains a single circular DNA molecule, a few RNA molecules, 70S ribosomes and the components needed for protein synthesis. Mitochondria divide by fission. Function: site of aerobic respiration; produces cellular energy as ATP, hence the power house of the cell.

Chloroplast: lens-shaped, oval, spherical, discoid or ribbon-like, 5–10 µm long and 2–4 µm wide, found in the mesophyll cells of leaves. Double membrane, the inner being less permeable. The space inside the inner membrane is the stroma, which contains flattened membranous sacs, the thylakoids, stacked as grana (40–60 per chloroplast) and connected by stroma lamellae. The stroma contains enzymes for carbohydrate and protein synthesis, double-stranded circular DNA and 70S ribosomes; chlorophyll is in the thylakoid membranes. Function: photosynthesis, trapping light energy (thylakoids) and synthesising carbohydrates (stroma).

Common characteristics: both are double membrane bound, both have their own circular DNA and 70S ribosomes, both divide by fission, so both are semi-autonomous organelles.

Draw the two labelled diagrams as described in the diagrams section: mitochondrion (outer membrane, inner membrane, cristae, matrix, DNA, ribosomes) and chloroplast (outer membrane, inner membrane, stroma, granum, thylakoid, stroma lamella, DNA, ribosomes).

ncert_questions.q: What are the characteristics of prokaryotic cells?
ncert_questions.a:
(i) Prokaryotic cells are generally small (1–10 µm) and multiply rapidly; examples are bacteria, cyanobacteria, mycoplasma and PPLO.
(ii) A cell wall surrounds the plasma membrane (except in mycoplasma); the three-layered cell envelope consists of glycocalyx, cell wall and plasma membrane.
(iii) There is no well-defined nucleus: the genomic DNA is a single, naked, circular molecule not enclosed by a nuclear membrane.
(iv) Many bacteria have extra circular DNA, the plasmids, which confer characters such as antibiotic resistance.
(v) Membrane-bound organelles are absent; the only membranous structures are mesosomes (extensions of the plasma membrane) and, in cyanobacteria, chromatophores.
(vi) Ribosomes are 70S (50S + 30S) and may form polysomes on an mRNA.
(vii) Reserve material is stored as inclusion bodies, which are not membrane bound: phosphate, cyanophycean and glycogen granules, gas vacuoles.
(viii) Motile forms have flagella made of filament, hook and basal body; pili and fimbriae are surface structures for attachment.

ncert_questions.q: Multicellular organisms have division of labour. Explain.
ncert_questions.a: A multicellular organism is made of many cells that are not all alike. Groups of similar cells are organised into tissues, tissues into organs and organs into organ systems, and each is specialised to perform a particular function. For example, in the human body muscle cells contract, nerve cells conduct impulses, red blood cells carry oxygen and gland cells secrete; in a plant, mesophyll cells photosynthesise, xylem conducts water and root hairs absorb it. No single cell performs all functions; the work of the body is divided among different types of cells, tissues and organs. This distribution of different functions among specialised cells is called division of labour. It makes the organism efficient, because each cell type can be structurally adapted to one job, but it also makes the cells dependent on one another, which is why a cell of a multicellular organism cannot live independently as a unicellular organism can.

ncert_questions.q: Cell is the basic unit of life. Discuss in brief.
ncert_questions.a: The cell is called the basic unit of life because: (i) every living organism, from a bacterium to a whale, is composed of cells and the products of cells (cell theory); (ii) the cell is the smallest unit that shows all the characteristics of life: metabolism, growth, response to stimuli and reproduction; anything smaller, such as an organelle, cannot survive independently; (iii) a unicellular organism carries out all life activities within a single cell, showing that one cell is sufficient for independent existence; (iv) in a multicellular organism all the functions of the body are the sum of the activities of its cells, and the cells show division of labour; (v) new cells arise only from pre-existing cells (Virchow), so the continuity of life passes through cells; and (vi) the genetic material that controls all activities and heredity is contained within the cell, in the nucleus or nucleoid. Hence the cell is both the structural and the functional unit of life.

ncert_questions.q: What are nuclear pores? State their function.
ncert_questions.a: Nuclear pores are minute openings in the nuclear envelope formed at places where the outer and inner nuclear membranes fuse with each other. Function: they are the passages through which RNA (mRNA, tRNA, rRNA) and protein molecules move in both directions between the nucleus and the cytoplasm. RNA and ribosomal subunits made in the nucleus pass out to the cytoplasm, and proteins such as histones, enzymes and ribosomal proteins made in the cytoplasm pass into the nucleus.

ncert_questions.q: Both lysosomes and vacuoles are endomembrane structures, yet they differ in terms of their functions. Comment.
ncert_questions.a:
Both are single-membrane-bound structures included in the endomembrane system, but their contents and roles differ.

Lysosomes are small vesicles formed by packaging in the Golgi apparatus. They contain hydrolytic enzymes (lipases, proteases, carbohydrases) that are optimally active at acidic pH. Their function is intracellular digestion: they digest carbohydrates, proteins, lipids and nucleic acids, break down worn-out organelles and food taken in by endocytosis, and destroy the cell itself when the enzymes are released (suicide bags).

Vacuoles are larger membrane-bound spaces bounded by the tonoplast. They contain water, sap, excretory products and other materials not useful to the cell. Their function is storage and osmoregulation: in plant cells they occupy up to 90 per cent of the cell volume and maintain turgidity, and the tonoplast moves ions and other materials into the vacuole against their concentration gradient; in Amoeba the contractile vacuole excretes water, and in protists food vacuoles hold engulfed food particles.

So lysosomes are digestive organelles while vacuoles are storage and osmoregulatory organelles.

ncert_questions.q: Describe the structure of the following with the help of labelled diagrams. (i) Nucleus (ii) Centrosome
ncert_questions.a:
(i) Nucleus: The nucleus is bounded by the nuclear envelope made of two parallel membranes separated by the perinuclear space of 10–50 nm. The outer membrane is continuous with the endoplasmic reticulum and bears ribosomes. The envelope is interrupted by nuclear pores formed by fusion of the two membranes, through which RNA and proteins pass. Inside is the nucleoplasm containing one or more nucleoli, spherical non-membrane-bound bodies that are the site of ribosomal RNA synthesis, and the chromatin, nucleoprotein fibres of DNA, histone and non-histone proteins and RNA, which condense into chromosomes during division. Draw the nucleus as described in the diagrams section and label nuclear envelope, perinuclear space, nuclear pore, nucleoplasm, nucleolus, chromatin and the ER continuous with the outer membrane.

(ii) Centrosome: The centrosome is a non-membranous organelle of animal cells containing two cylindrical centrioles lying perpendicular to each other, surrounded by amorphous pericentriolar material. Each centriole has a cartwheel organisation: nine evenly spaced peripheral fibrils of tubulin, each fibril a triplet of microtubules, adjacent triplets being linked. The centre of the proximal region has a proteinaceous hub connected to the peripheral triplets by radial spokes. There are no central microtubules (9+0). The centrioles form the basal bodies of cilia and flagella and the spindle fibres during cell division. Draw the T.S. of a centriole (nine triplets, hub, spokes) and the two centrioles at right angles.

ncert_questions.q: What is a centromere? How does the position of centromere form the basis of classification of chromosomes? Support your answer with a diagram showing the position of centromere on different types of chromosomes.
ncert_questions.a:
The centromere is the primary constriction of a chromosome, the narrow region that holds the two sister chromatids together and on whose sides lie the disc-shaped kinetochores to which spindle fibres attach during cell division.

On the basis of the position of the centromere, chromosomes are classified into four types:
(i) Metacentric: centromere in the middle, forming two equal arms.
(ii) Sub-metacentric: centromere slightly away from the middle, resulting in one shorter arm and one longer arm.
(iii) Acrocentric: centromere close to one end, forming one extremely short arm and one very long arm.
(iv) Telocentric: centromere at the terminal end of the chromosome.

A few chromosomes also have a non-staining secondary constriction at a constant location, which gives the appearance of a small fragment called the satellite. Draw the four chromosomes as in the diagrams section, with the centromere in the middle, off-centre, near the end and at the tip, each labelled.

ncert_questions.q: What is the difference between rough endoplasmic reticulum and smooth endoplasmic reticulum?
ncert_questions.a:
RER: bears ribosomes on its outer surface, hence rough; mainly cisternae; extensive and continuous with the outer nuclear membrane; abundant in cells actively synthesising and secreting proteins (pancreatic acinar cells, plasma cells); function: protein synthesis and secretion.
SER: no ribosomes, hence smooth; mainly tubules; not continuous with the nucleus; abundant in cells synthesising lipids and steroids (liver, adrenal cortex, testis); function: lipid synthesis and, in animal cells, synthesis of steroidal hormones; also detoxification in liver cells.

ncert_questions.q: What does 'S' refer to in a 70S and an 80S ribosome?
ncert_questions.a: S stands for the Svedberg unit, the sedimentation coefficient, which measures the rate at which a particle sediments when centrifuged in an ultracentrifuge. It is indirectly a measure of the size and density of the particle. Because it depends on shape and density as well as mass, the values are not additive: a 50S and a 30S subunit form a 70S ribosome and a 60S and a 40S subunit form an 80S ribosome.

pyq.q: Which of the following statements about the cell theory is incorrect?
options: It was proposed by Schleiden and Schwann
It states that all living organisms are composed of cells and products of cells
It was modified by Virchow, who said that new cells arise from pre-existing cells
It was first proposed by Robert Hooke after observing cork
pyq.answer: d
pyq.solution: Hooke saw cork cells and coined the term 'cell' but did not propose the cell theory; Schleiden and Schwann did, and Virchow added Omnis cellula-e cellula.

pyq.q: Which one of the following is not a membrane-bound organelle?
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: Ribosomes are granular structures of RNA and protein with no membrane around them; the other three are single-membrane-bound organelles of the endomembrane system.

pyq.q: The fluid mosaic model of the plasma membrane was proposed by
pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: Singer and Nicolson proposed the fluid mosaic model in 1972: a quasi-fluid lipid bilayer with proteins that can move laterally.

pyq.q: The site of active ribosomal RNA synthesis in a eukaryotic cell is the
pyq.answer: a
pyq.solution: The nucleolus, a non-membrane-bound body in the nucleoplasm, is the site of rRNA synthesis; cells active in protein synthesis have larger nucleoli.

pyq.q: The arrangement of microtubules in the axoneme of a cilium is
pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: The axoneme has nine peripheral doublets and two central singlet microtubules (9+2); the centriole has nine triplets and no central tubules (9+0).

pyq.q: A chromosome in which the centromere is situated close to one end, forming one extremely short arm and one very long arm, is called
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: Acrocentric chromosomes have the centromere close to the end; telocentric have it at the very tip; sub-metacentric have it slightly off-centre.

pyq.q: Which of the following is a common feature of plant sieve tube cells and mammalian red blood cells?
options: Absence of a nucleus at maturity
pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: Both are enucleate at maturity though they had a nucleus during development; this is NCERT's own example of cells lacking a nucleus.

pyq.q: Inclusion bodies of prokaryotic cells are
options: reserve materials lying free in the cytoplasm without a membrane
extensions of the plasma membrane into the cell
pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: Inclusion bodies (phosphate, cyanophycean and glycogen granules, gas vacuoles) are stored reserve material not bound by any membrane; option (c) describes mesosomes and (d) chromatophores.

pyq.q: The cell wall of fungi is made of
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: Fungal walls are made of chitin; plant walls of cellulose, hemicellulose, pectin and protein; bacterial walls of peptidoglycan; calcium pectate forms the middle lamella.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): Mitochondria and chloroplasts are called semi-autonomous organelles. Reason (R): They possess their own circular DNA, RNA and 70S ribosomes and divide by fission.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: a
pyq.solution: Because they carry their own genetic material and protein-synthesising machinery and divide independently, these organelles are semi-autonomous; R explains A.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): Rough endoplasmic reticulum is abundant in cells that are actively secreting proteins. Reason (R): Ribosomes attached to the RER synthesise proteins that enter the ER lumen for secretion.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
