A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: a
pyq.solution: RER is frequently observed in cells actively involved in protein synthesis and secretion, precisely because its ribosomes make proteins destined for secretion.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): The plasma membrane is described as quasi-fluid. Reason (R): Proteins in the membrane can move laterally within the lipid bilayer, and this fluidity is important for cell growth, secretion, endocytosis and cell division.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: a
pyq.solution: The quasi-fluid nature of the lipid bilayer enables lateral movement of proteins; the fluid mosaic model attributes the listed functions to this fluidity.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): Mesosomes are membrane-bound organelles of prokaryotic cells. Reason (R): Mesosomes are formed by extensions of the plasma membrane into the cell as vesicles, tubules and lamellae.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: d
pyq.solution: Prokaryotes have no membrane-bound organelles; the mesosome is not an independent organelle but an infolding of the plasma membrane, which is what R correctly states.

pyq.q: Name the three layers of the cell envelope of a bacterium in order from outside to inside. On what basis are bacteria classified as gram positive and gram negative?
pyq.answer:
From outside to inside: glycocalyx (slime layer or capsule), cell wall and plasma membrane. The three layers act together as a single protective unit.

Bacteria are classified on the basis of differences in their cell envelope and their response to the Gram staining procedure: bacteria that take up (retain) the Gram stain are gram positive and those that do not are gram negative.

pyq.q: What is a polysome? What is its advantage to the cell?
pyq.answer: A polysome or polyribosome is a chain of several ribosomes attached to a single mRNA molecule. The ribosomes of the polysome translate the same mRNA simultaneously, so many copies of the same polypeptide are produced from one mRNA in a short time, which is economical and rapid for the cell.

pyq.q: Distinguish between cilia and flagella, giving two differences.
pyq.answer:
(i) Cilia are small and short; flagella are comparatively longer.
(ii) Cilia are numerous on a cell and beat like oars to move the cell or the surrounding fluid (Paramecium, tracheal epithelium); flagella are few (usually one or two) and move the cell by whip-like undulation (sperm, Euglena).
Both have the same 9+2 axoneme covered by the plasma membrane and arise from basal bodies.

pyq.q: What is a tonoplast? State one function.
pyq.answer: The tonoplast is the single membrane that bounds the vacuole of a plant cell. Function: it facilitates the transport of a number of ions and other materials into the vacuole against their concentration gradient, so that their concentration in the vacuole becomes much higher than in the cytoplasm; this maintains the turgidity of the cell.

pyq.q: Name the scientist who first described the nucleus and the one who named chromatin. What is the perinuclear space?
pyq.answer: Robert Brown first described the nucleus (1831); Flemming gave the name chromatin to the nuclear material stained by basic dyes. The perinuclear space is the gap of 10 to 50 nm between the two parallel membranes of the nuclear envelope.

pyq.q: Describe the fluid mosaic model of the plasma membrane. Why is the fluid nature of the membrane important?
pyq.answer:
According to the fluid mosaic model (Singer and Nicolson, 1972) the plasma membrane is a lipid bilayer of phosphoglycerides with their polar heads facing the outer sides and their hydrophobic tails facing inward, so the non-polar tails are protected from the aqueous environment. Cholesterol is also present. Proteins are embedded in this bilayer like tiles of a mosaic: integral proteins are partially or totally buried in the membrane and peripheral proteins lie on its surface. Carbohydrates are attached to some lipids and proteins on the outer surface (1–5 per cent). The lipid bilayer is quasi-fluid, which enables the lateral movement of proteins within it; this ability to move is the fluidity of the membrane. The erythrocyte membrane has about 52 per cent protein and 40 per cent lipid.

Importance of fluidity: it makes possible cell growth, formation of intercellular junctions, secretion, endocytosis and cell division, and it allows the membrane to reseal and to rearrange its proteins for selective transport.

pyq.q: State the functions of the Golgi apparatus. Why is it always found in close association with the endoplasmic reticulum?
pyq.answer:
Functions: (i) The Golgi apparatus principally performs the function of packaging materials, to be delivered either to intracellular targets (for example lysosomes) or secreted outside the cell. (ii) Proteins synthesised by ribosomes on the ER are modified in the cisternae before being released from the trans face. (iii) It is the important site of formation of glycoproteins and glycolipids (glycosylation). (iv) It forms lysosomes and secretory vesicles.

Association with ER: Materials to be packaged in the form of vesicles from the ER fuse with the cis (forming) face of the Golgi and move towards the trans (maturing) face. Since the Golgi receives its raw material from the ER continuously, it must remain close to the ER; the cisternae are concentrically arranged near the nucleus with the convex cis face towards the ER.

pyq.q: Give three differences between a prokaryotic cell and a eukaryotic cell.
pyq.answer:
(i) Nucleus: Prokaryotic cell has no nuclear membrane; the genomic DNA is naked and circular. Eukaryotic cell has a true nucleus bounded by a double-membrane nuclear envelope, with nucleolus and linear chromosomes associated with histones.
(ii) Organelles: Prokaryotic cell has no membrane-bound organelles, only mesosomes and chromatophores formed from the plasma membrane. Eukaryotic cell has ER, Golgi, lysosomes, mitochondria, plastids, vacuoles and microbodies.
(iii) Ribosomes: 70S (50S + 30S) in prokaryotes; 80S (60S + 40S) in the eukaryotic cytoplasm.
(iv) Cell wall: peptidoglycan in bacteria; cellulose in plants, chitin in fungi, absent in animals.
(v) Flagella: filament, hook and basal body in prokaryotes; 9+2 axoneme covered by plasma membrane in eukaryotes.
(vi) Size and division: prokaryotes small (1–10 µm), divide by fission; eukaryotes larger (10–100 µm), divide by mitosis and meiosis.

pyq.q: Which cell organelles are included in the endomembrane system? Why are mitochondria, chloroplasts and peroxisomes not included in it, although they are membrane-bound?
pyq.answer:
The endomembrane system includes the endoplasmic reticulum, Golgi complex, lysosomes and vacuoles. These organelles are grouped together because their functions are coordinated: proteins and lipids made in the ER are transported in vesicles to the cis face of the Golgi, modified and packaged there, and released from the trans face as lysosomes, secretory vesicles or material for the vacuole; the membranes of all of them are continuous or exchange material through vesicles.

Mitochondria, chloroplasts and peroxisomes are membrane-bound, but their functions (aerobic respiration, photosynthesis and oxidative reactions respectively) are not coordinated with the ER-Golgi-lysosome-vacuole pathway, and they do not exchange vesicles with it. Mitochondria and chloroplasts also have their own DNA and ribosomes and divide independently. Hence they are not considered part of the endomembrane system.

pyq.q: Describe the structure of a centriole with the help of a labelled diagram.
pyq.answer: The centrosome contains two cylindrical centrioles lying perpendicular to each other, surrounded by amorphous pericentriolar material. In transverse section each centriole shows a cartwheel organisation: nine evenly spaced peripheral fibrils of tubulin protein, each fibril being a triplet of microtubules, with adjacent triplets linked to each other. The central part of the proximal region is a proteinaceous hub, connected to the tubules of the peripheral triplets by protein radial spokes. There are no central microtubules (9+0), and there is no membrane. The centrioles form the basal bodies of cilia and flagella and the spindle fibres of the spindle apparatus during cell division in animal cells. (Draw the T.S. as in the diagrams section: nine triplets, hub, radial spokes, linkers; and the two centrioles at right angles.)

pyq.q: Draw a labelled diagram of a mitochondrion and describe its structure. Why is it called the power house of the cell?
pyq.answer:
Diagram: as in the diagrams section, a sausage-shaped organelle with outer membrane, inner membrane folded into cristae, outer compartment, matrix with circular DNA and ribosomes.

Structure: Mitochondria are typically sausage-shaped or cylindrical, 1.0–4.1 µm in length and 0.2–1.0 µm (average 0.5 µm) in diameter; the number per cell varies with the physiological activity of the cell, and they are not easily seen unless stained (Janus green). Each is a double membrane-bound structure. The outer membrane forms the continuous limiting boundary of the organelle. The inner membrane is thrown into a number of infoldings called cristae that project into the matrix and increase the surface area. The two membranes divide the lumen into two aqueous compartments, the outer compartment (between the membranes) and the inner compartment filled with a dense homogeneous substance, the matrix. The two membranes have their own specific enzymes. The matrix possesses a single circular DNA molecule, a few RNA molecules, 70S ribosomes and the components required for protein synthesis; mitochondria divide by fission and are therefore semi-autonomous.

Power house: Mitochondria are the sites of aerobic respiration. The enzymes of the Krebs cycle lie in the matrix and the electron transport chain lies on the inner membrane and cristae. The energy released by the oxidation of food is used to synthesise ATP by oxidative phosphorylation, and ATP is the energy currency used for all cellular work. Since almost all the usable energy of the cell is produced here, the mitochondrion is called the power house of the cell.

pyq.q: Draw a labelled diagram of a chloroplast and describe its structure. Name the three types of plastids and state what each contains.
pyq.answer:
Diagram: as in the diagrams section, lens-shaped with outer and inner membranes, stroma, grana of stacked thylakoids, stroma lamellae, DNA and ribosomes.

Structure: Chloroplasts are found chiefly in the mesophyll cells of leaves. They are lens-shaped, oval, spherical, discoid or ribbon-like, 5–10 µm long and 2–4 µm wide; their number varies from one per cell in the green alga Chlamydomonas to 20–40 per mesophyll cell. Each is bounded by a double membrane, of which the inner membrane is relatively less permeable. The space enclosed by the inner membrane is filled with the stroma. In the stroma lie a number of organised flattened membranous sacs, the thylakoids, arranged in stacks like piles of coins called grana (40–60 per chloroplast). Flat membranous tubules, the stroma lamellae, connect the thylakoids of different grana. The thylakoid membrane encloses a space called the lumen. The chlorophyll and carotenoid pigments are located in the thylakoid membranes, where the light reactions occur. The stroma contains the enzymes for the synthesis of carbohydrates (dark reactions) and proteins, a double-stranded circular DNA and 70S ribosomes, which make the chloroplast semi-autonomous.

Types of plastids: (i) Chloroplasts contain chlorophyll and carotenoid pigments that trap light energy for photosynthesis. (ii) Chromoplasts contain fat-soluble carotenoid pigments such as carotene and xanthophylls, giving yellow, orange or red colour to petals and fruits. (iii) Leucoplasts are colourless plastids that store nutrients: amyloplasts store starch (potato), elaioplasts store oils and fats, aleuroplasts store proteins.

pyq.q: Describe the structure of a bacterial cell with the help of a labelled diagram, covering the cell envelope, the genetic material, the ribosomes and the surface structures.
pyq.answer:
Diagram: as in the diagrams section, showing capsule, cell wall, plasma membrane, mesosome, nucleoid, plasmid, ribosomes, inclusion bodies, flagellum, pili and fimbriae.

Cell envelope: a three-layered structure of outer glycocalyx (a loose slime layer or a thick, tough capsule), middle cell wall, which determines the shape and gives structural support, and inner selectively permeable plasma membrane. On the basis of the envelope and the response to Gram staining, bacteria are gram positive or gram negative. The plasma membrane extends into the cell as vesicles, tubules and lamellae to form the mesosome, which helps in cell wall formation, DNA replication and distribution, respiration and secretion. Cyanobacteria also have pigment-bearing chromatophores.

Genetic material: a single, naked, circular genomic DNA lying in the cytoplasm as the nucleoid, with no nuclear membrane, and often small circular plasmids that confer characters such as antibiotic resistance.

Ribosomes and inclusion bodies: 70S ribosomes (50S + 30S, about 15 nm by 20 nm) associated with the plasma membrane, often forming polysomes on an mRNA. Reserve material is stored as non-membranous inclusion bodies: phosphate granules, cyanophycean granules, glycogen granules and, in photosynthetic bacteria, gas vacuoles.

Surface structures: motile bacteria have flagella composed of a filament (the longest part, outside the cell), a hook and a basal body; pili are elongated tubular protein structures and fimbriae are small bristle-like fibres that attach the bacterium to rocks or host tissues; neither is used for movement. There are no membrane-bound organelles.

pyq.q: Describe the structure of the nucleus with a labelled diagram. Explain how chromosomes are classified on the basis of the position of the centromere.
pyq.answer:
Diagram: as in the diagrams section: nuclear envelope with two membranes, perinuclear space, nuclear pores, ER continuous with the outer membrane, nucleoplasm, nucleolus, chromatin.

Structure: The nucleus (first described by Robert Brown, 1831) is bounded by the nuclear envelope of two parallel membranes separated by the perinuclear space (10–50 nm), which forms a barrier between the nucleoplasm and the cytoplasm. The outer membrane is continuous with the ER and bears ribosomes. The envelope is interrupted at places by nuclear pores, formed by fusion of the two membranes, through which RNA and proteins move in both directions. The nucleoplasm contains one or more nucleoli, spherical bodies without a membrane that are the site of active rRNA synthesis, and the chromatin, an extended network of nucleoprotein fibres of DNA, basic histone proteins, non-histone proteins and RNA (named by Flemming). During cell division the chromatin condenses into chromosomes; a human cell has about 2 m of DNA in 46 chromosomes. Mature mammalian RBCs and sieve tube cells lack a nucleus.

Classification of chromosomes: every chromosome has a primary constriction, the centromere, bearing disc-shaped kinetochores. By its position: metacentric, centromere in the middle, two equal arms; sub-metacentric, centromere slightly away from the middle, one shorter and one longer arm; acrocentric, centromere close to the end, one extremely short and one very long arm; telocentric, terminal centromere. Some chromosomes also have a non-staining secondary constriction at a constant location, producing a satellite.

pyq.q:
A student examined electron micrographs of two cells. Cell P showed an extensive network of membranes studded with ribosomes, a large stack of flattened sacs near the nucleus and many small vesicles rich in hydrolytic enzymes. Cell Q showed no nuclear membrane, a single circular DNA molecule lying free in the cytoplasm, a few infoldings of the plasma membrane and granules not surrounded by any membrane.
(i) Identify cell P and cell Q as prokaryotic or eukaryotic and give one reason each.
(ii) Name the ribosome-studded network and the stack of flattened sacs in cell P and state the function of each.
(iii) Name the infoldings of the plasma membrane in cell Q and give two of their functions.
(iv) What are the membrane-less granules in cell Q called? Give two examples.
pyq.answer:
(i) Cell P is eukaryotic because it has membrane-bound organelles (ER, Golgi, lysosomes) and a nucleus. Cell Q is prokaryotic because it has no nuclear membrane and its genomic DNA lies naked in the cytoplasm.
(ii) The network is the rough endoplasmic reticulum, which synthesises proteins for secretion; the stack of flattened sacs is the Golgi apparatus, which packages and modifies these proteins (glycosylation) and forms lysosomes and secretory vesicles. Cell P is evidently a secretory cell.
(iii) The infoldings are mesosomes. They help in cell wall formation, DNA replication and its distribution to daughter cells, respiration and secretion, and they increase the surface area and enzyme content of the plasma membrane. (Any two.)
(iv) They are inclusion bodies, reserve materials not bound by a membrane; examples are phosphate granules, cyanophycean granules, glycogen granules and gas vacuoles.

pyq.q:
The plasma membrane of a red blood cell was analysed and found to contain about 52 per cent protein and 40 per cent lipid. When the membrane was warmed slightly, labelled proteins on one side of the cell were seen to spread over the entire surface within minutes. Glucose entered the cell only when a specific membrane protein was present, while oxygen entered freely; sodium ions were pumped out even though their concentration outside was already higher.
(i) Name the model of membrane structure supported by the movement of the labelled proteins and the scientists who proposed it.
(ii) Why can oxygen cross the membrane freely while glucose needs a protein? Name the type of transport in each case.
(iii) What kind of transport moves sodium out of the cell? What does it require?
(iv) Name the main lipid of the membrane and state how its molecules are arranged.
pyq.answer:
(i) The fluid mosaic model, proposed by Singer and Nicolson (1972); the spreading of labelled proteins shows the lateral movement of proteins in a quasi-fluid bilayer.
(ii) Oxygen is a small neutral (non-polar) molecule and dissolves through the hydrophobic lipid bilayer by simple diffusion along its concentration gradient (passive transport). Glucose is a polar molecule and cannot pass through the non-polar interior; it needs a carrier protein, which is facilitated diffusion, still passive and along the gradient.
(iii) Active transport, because sodium is moved against its concentration gradient (from lower to higher concentration). It requires energy in the form of ATP and a specific pump protein, the Na+/K+ pump.
(iv) The main lipids are phosphoglycerides (phospholipids). They form a bilayer with the polar (hydrophilic) heads facing the outer surfaces and the hydrophobic tails facing inward, protected from the aqueous environment; cholesterol is also present.

practice_mcq.q: Who first saw and described a live cell?
practice_mcq.explanation: Leeuwenhoek first saw and described a live cell; Hooke saw dead cork cells; Brown discovered the nucleus.

practice_mcq.q: The smallest cell known is that of
practice_mcq.explanation: Mycoplasmas are only about 0.3 µm long; bacteria are 3–5 µm and RBCs about 7 µm.

practice_mcq.q: Which of the following organisms is a prokaryote?
practice_mcq.explanation: Anabaena is a cyanobacterium (blue-green alga), a prokaryote; the other three are eukaryotes.

practice_mcq.q: A bacterial flagellum consists of
options: Axoneme, central sheath and basal body
Nine doublets and two central microtubules
practice_mcq.explanation: The bacterial flagellum has three parts, filament, hook and basal body, and is structurally different from the 9+2 eukaryotic flagellum.

practice_mcq.q: The ribosomes present in the matrix of mitochondria are
practice_mcq.explanation: Mitochondria and chloroplasts contain 70S ribosomes of the prokaryotic type; cytoplasmic eukaryotic ribosomes are 80S.

practice_mcq.q: In the erythrocyte plasma membrane the approximate proportions of protein and lipid are
practice_mcq.explanation: NCERT: the erythrocyte membrane has approximately 52 per cent protein and 40 per cent lipid.

practice_mcq.q: The middle lamella between adjacent plant cells is composed mainly of
practice_mcq.explanation: The middle lamella is a layer mainly of calcium pectate that glues neighbouring cells together.

practice_mcq.q: Which of the following is not a part of the endomembrane system?
practice_mcq.explanation: Mitochondria, chloroplasts and peroxisomes are excluded because their functions are not coordinated with ER, Golgi, lysosomes and vacuoles.

practice_mcq.q: Steroidal hormones in animal cells are synthesised in the
practice_mcq.explanation: SER is the major site of lipid synthesis, and lipid-like steroidal hormones are made in the SER of animal cells.

practice_mcq.q: The Golgi apparatus was first observed by
practice_mcq.explanation: Camillo Golgi observed densely stained reticular structures near the nucleus in 1898.

practice_mcq.q: The hydrolytic enzymes of lysosomes are optimally active at
practice_mcq.explanation: Lysosomal hydrolases (lipases, proteases, carbohydrases) work best at acidic pH.

practice_mcq.q: In plant cells the vacuole may occupy up to what fraction of the cell volume?
practice_mcq.explanation: NCERT states that in plant cells the vacuoles can occupy up to 90 per cent of the volume of the cell.

practice_mcq.q: Which plastid stores oils and fats?
practice_mcq.explanation: Elaioplasts store oils and fats; amyloplasts store starch, aleuroplasts store proteins and chromoplasts hold carotenoid pigments.

practice_mcq.q: Stroma lamellae are
options: Flat membranous tubules connecting the thylakoids of different grana
Infoldings of the inner membrane of mitochondria
practice_mcq.explanation: Stroma lamellae connect the thylakoids of different grana; stacks of thylakoids are grana; inner mitochondrial folds are cristae.

practice_mcq.q: Ribosomes were first observed under the electron microscope by
practice_mcq.explanation: George Palade (1953) observed ribosomes as dense particles under the electron microscope.

practice_mcq.q: The number of radial spokes in the axoneme of a cilium is
practice_mcq.explanation: The central sheath is connected to one tubule of each of the nine peripheral doublets by a radial spoke, so there are nine radial spokes.

practice_mcq.q: Each peripheral fibril of a centriole is a
practice_mcq.explanation: The centriole has nine evenly spaced peripheral fibrils of tubulin, each a triplet, arranged like a cartwheel around a hub.

practice_mcq.q: The width of the perinuclear space is about
practice_mcq.explanation: The two membranes of the nuclear envelope are separated by a perinuclear space of 10 to 50 nm.

practice_mcq.q: A chromosome with a terminal centromere is called
practice_mcq.explanation: Telocentric chromosomes have the centromere at the terminal end; acrocentric ones have it close to, but not at, the end.

practice_mcq.q: Which of the following statements about nucleoli is correct?
options: They are bounded by a single membrane
They are the site of ribosomal RNA synthesis
They contain the plasmids of the cell
They are found only in prokaryotes
practice_mcq.explanation: Nucleoli are non-membrane-bound bodies in the nucleoplasm, and their content is continuous with it; they are the site of active rRNA synthesis.

practice_mcq.q: Which of the following is present in a plant cell but absent in an animal cell?
practice_mcq.explanation: Plastids (and the cell wall and a large central vacuole) are found in plant cells; centrioles are characteristic of animal cells; mitochondria occur in both.

common_mistakes: Crediting Robert Brown with discovering the cell. He discovered the nucleus (1831); Leeuwenhoek first saw a live cell and Hooke coined the word from cork. NCERT exercise 1 is set on exactly this error.

Calling mesosomes or inclusion bodies 'membrane-bound organelles' of prokaryotes. Prokaryotes have none; the mesosome is an infolding of the plasma membrane and inclusion bodies lie free without any membrane.

Writing 50S + 30S = 80S, or saying eukaryotic ribosomes are 70S. Prokaryotes: 70S (50S + 30S); eukaryotic cytoplasm: 80S (60S + 40S); mitochondria and chloroplasts: 70S. S is a sedimentation coefficient and is not additive.

Swapping doublets and triplets: the axoneme of cilia and flagella has nine doublets plus two central singlets (9+2); the centriole has nine triplets and no central tubules (9+0) with a hub and spokes.

Confusing cristae, cisternae and thylakoids in the match-the-following question. Cristae are inner-membrane folds of mitochondria, cisternae are the flattened sacs of the Golgi, thylakoids are the flattened sacs in the chloroplast stroma.

Leaving the fluid mosaic answer at 'lipids and proteins'. The marking scheme wants the bilayer orientation (polar heads out, hydrophobic tails in), integral versus peripheral proteins, the word quasi-fluid, lateral movement and the names Singer and Nicolson (1972).

Saying the cell wall is selectively permeable, or giving cellulose for fungi and chitin for plants. Selective permeability belongs to the plasma membrane; fungal walls are chitin, plant walls cellulose, algal walls cellulose plus galactans, mannans and calcium carbonate.

Including mitochondria and chloroplasts in the endomembrane system. NCERT lists only ER, Golgi, lysosomes and vacuoles; mitochondria, chloroplasts and peroxisomes are excluded because their functions are not coordinated with these.

Drawing the mitochondrion with cristae from the outer membrane, or the chloroplast without stroma lamellae. Both diagrams must show two membranes, and the grana must be connected by stroma lamellae with the stroma labelled separately.

Describing the nucleolus as membrane-bound, or the nuclear envelope as a single membrane. The nucleolus has no membrane; the envelope has two membranes with a 10–50 nm perinuclear space and pores where the two fuse.
strategy:
This chapter is memory-heavy but the memory is organised: every organelle is asked in the same four-part way, structure, diagram, function, and one distinguishing number or name. Prepare it organelle by organelle on a single sheet with those four columns and you have covered eighty per cent of the questions.

Start with the timeline of discoveries and the cell theory; that is the first MCQ of almost every paper and takes twenty minutes to fix. Then do the prokaryotic cell as one labelled diagram (bacterial cell) and one list (characteristics of prokaryotes, NCERT exercise 8). Next spend the most time on the four diagrams that carry five marks each: mitochondrion, chloroplast, nucleus, and the fluid mosaic model. Draw each one from memory three times until every NCERT label comes out without prompting, and write the numbers under each (sizes, 40–60 grana, 10–50 nm, 52 per cent protein). Then learn the endomembrane system as a flow, ER to Golgi (cis to trans) to lysosome or secretory vesicle, and be able to say why mitochondria and peroxisomes are left out.

For the 1-mark and 2-mark items, keep a list of exceptions: mycoplasma (smallest, no wall), RBC and sieve tube (no nucleus), Chlamydomonas (one chloroplast), euglenoids (plastids outside plants), bacterial flagellum (no 9+2). For the 3-mark items, practise the standard tables: prokaryote versus eukaryote, plant cell versus animal cell, RER versus SER, lysosome versus vacuole, cilia versus flagella, axoneme versus centriole.

Solve all fourteen NCERT exercise questions in writing; exercises 3, 5, 6, 7, 11, 12, 13 and 14 are lifted into school papers almost unchanged. Then go through the exemplar MCQs, which are the template for NEET questions from this chapter. In the exam, budget the 5-mark diagram question first: a clean labelled diagram with the numbers written beneath earns marks even before the description begins.

I know who first saw a live cell, who named the cell, who discovered the nucleus, who named chromatin, who saw the Golgi and who saw ribosomes.
I can arrange Mycoplasma, bacteria, human RBC and the ostrich egg by size with their numbers.
I can draw and label a bacterial cell and describe the three layers of the cell envelope, gram staining, mesosome, plasmid, flagellum parts, pili and fimbriae.
I can define inclusion bodies with three examples and say why they are not organelles.
I can write 70S = 50S + 30S and 80S = 60S + 40S, explain the S, and say where 70S ribosomes occur in a eukaryotic cell.
I can draw the fluid mosaic model with polar heads, hydrophobic tails, integral and peripheral proteins, and explain passive, facilitated and active transport with the Na+/K+ pump.
I can give the cell wall composition of algae, plants and fungi, the middle lamella, primary and secondary walls, and plasmodesmata.
I can list the four members of the endomembrane system and explain why mitochondria, chloroplasts and peroxisomes are excluded.
I can distinguish RER from SER, describe the Golgi with cis and trans faces and glycosylation, and compare lysosomes with vacuoles including the tonoplast.
I can draw a mitochondrion with its dimensions, cristae, matrix, DNA and 70S ribosomes, and explain 'power house' and 'semi-autonomous'.
I can draw a chloroplast with grana, thylakoids, stroma lamellae and stroma, give its numbers, and name the three plastid types with what each stores.
I can draw the 9+2 axoneme with central sheath, nine radial spokes and interdoublet linkers, and the 9-triplet centriole with hub and spokes.
I can draw the nucleus with nuclear envelope, perinuclear space, pores, nucleolus and chromatin, and state the function of nuclear pores and the nucleolus.
I can classify chromosomes as metacentric, sub-metacentric, acrocentric and telocentric with a diagram and define centromere, kinetochore and satellite.
I can write five differences each between prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells and between plant and animal cells in table form.
